source: Zhang et al. (2025) Leveraging LLMs to Emulate the Design Processes of Different Cognitive Styles
finding: GPT-4o was prompted with zero-shot chain-of-thought to act as a problem-driven or solution-driven designer (Dorst and Cross taxonomy). Protocol coding (FBS) showed it reproduced the static split between the two styles.
numbers: Bathroom product task, with and without extra constraints. 10 generated processes per group (P1,P2,S1,S2) plus 10 baseline outputs (B1,B2). Without constraint: Formulation 31.7% (problem-driven) vs 16.3% (solution-driven), t=8.489, p<0.001; Structure 10.6 vs 29.3, p<0.001; Function 18.9 vs 9.2, p<0.001. Coder agreement 79.5%.
limits: One model (GPT-4o), one domain, N=10 per cell, human comparison is to numbers from prior studies (Chen et al. 2023), not a new human sample.
agent_relevance: A prompt can switch an LLM between solution-first and problem-first behaviour in a measurable way, so the style can be a scaffold knob.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Leveraging LLMs to Emulate the Design Processes of Different Cognitive Styles
finding: Emulated solution-driven runs spent most of their time iterating inside the solution space (SS transitions), as human solution-first designers do.
numbers: SS transitions: 29.4% (solution-driven) vs 9.9% (problem-driven) without constraint, t=-8.949, p<0.001; with constraint 27.9 vs 13.1, p<0.001. Reformulation-S 21.5 vs 5.8, p<0.001.
limits: Percent of coded segments. Constrained task weakened some contrasts (Be, PS, SP not significant).
agent_relevance: Solution-first conjecture-then-refine loops can be induced in an LLM and counted; good proxy metric for our logging.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Leveraging LLMs to Emulate the Design Processes of Different Cognitive Styles
finding: Key gap: the LLM did not show the back-and-forth between problem and solution spaces that marks human co-evolution. It stayed in one space and moved linearly.
numbers: Problem-driven emulation had fewer PS and SP transitions than solution-driven (p<0.01, unconstrained). PS: 6.7 vs 10.5, t=-3.83, p=0.001; SP: 6.4 vs 9.8, p=0.003. Human problem-driven designers show more flexible switching.
quote: LLMs lack the fully complex nonlinear transitions between problem and solution spaces observed in human designers.
limits: Authors say fine-tuning or Graph of Thoughts might fix this; not tested.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that single-pass CoT lacks the reframing loop (problem reformulated by solution). A schema operator that forces P-to-S-to-P turns is justified.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Leveraging LLMs to Emulate the Design Processes of Different Cognitive Styles
finding: Style-emulating prompts raised output quality over just asking GPT-4o for a design.
numbers: Novelty and integrity higher than baseline for both styles (p<0.05). Feasibility higher in all groups except P2 (problem-driven, constrained). Solution-driven designs scored higher integrity than problem-driven. Constrained baseline had lowest feasibility. Two expert raters, r=0.77.
limits: Scores read from a figure in the paper, not tabulated in the text. Small N=10 per group.
agent_relevance: Cheap scaffold: explicit solution-first instruction gives more complete designs; problem-first with hard constraints cost feasibility.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Leveraging LLMs to Emulate the Design Processes of Different Cognitive Styles
finding: P-S Index check: every problem-driven LLM run was classified problem-focused; all solution-driven runs were solution-focused except two under constraint.
numbers: P-S Index threshold 1.0. 20 of 20 problem-driven runs correct; 18 of 20 solution-driven runs correct (the two misses were in the constrained condition).
limits: Self-defined index; same coders.
agent_relevance: Gives a simple per-run diagnostic (ratio of problem-space to solution-space statements) to log in our agent.

source: Ege et al. (2024/2025) ChatGPT as an inventor: strengths and weaknesses of LLMs against humans in engineering design
finding: ChatGPT 4.0 acted as sole decision-maker for a team in a 48-hour Nerf-dart launcher hackathon against five graduate engineering teams. It placed 2nd of 6.
numbers: Distance fired: Team 3 37.66 m, ChatGPT 14.8 m, Team 2 8.07 m, Team 1 6.56 m, Team 4 5.06 m, Team 5 0.06 m. Average 12.0 m. 116 prototypes logged; ChatGPT made 16 (8 refinement, 7 exploration, 2 active learning). Chat: 97 prompts, 108 codes.
limits: One hackathon, one task, humans executed instructions, graduate students not novices vs experts. Single run per team.
agent_relevance: An LLM can run a whole concept-to-prototype loop at a roughly competent-student level, with humans as hands.

source: Ege et al. (2024/2025) ChatGPT as an inventor: strengths and weaknesses of LLMs against humans in engineering design
finding: The LLM proposed five working principles at once (pneumatic, spring, slingshot, gravity, centrifugal) but only built the three common ones. It went for the safe solution.
numbers: 5 principles listed; first suggestion was pneumatic, same as the winning team. Key finding 2 in paper.
limits: Authors' interpretation of intent, no repeated trials.
agent_relevance: Wide conjecture generation is cheap for the LLM; the choice step is conservative. Our agent needs a forced pick of one risky option.

source: Ege et al. (2024/2025) ChatGPT as an inventor: strengths and weaknesses of LLMs against humans in engineering design
finding: The LLM dropped the pneumatic concept after one setback (valves did not fit) and pivoted, treating a small failure as a dead end. The winning human team kept iterating the same concept.
numbers: Abandoned after 1 iteration. Winning pneumatic team reached 37.66 m, 2.5x the LLM.
quote: Alright, given the challenges with the pneumatic launcher, we might want to pivot to another mechanism
limits: Single case. Authors contrast with what an experienced human designer would do (not measured).
agent_relevance: Opposite of human fixation: premature abandonment. An expert-like scaffold needs a diagnose-before-pivot step.

source: Ege et al. (2024/2025) ChatGPT as an inventor: strengths and weaknesses of LLMs against humans in engineering design
finding: The LLM also showed design fixation in two ways: it clung to a working concept late, and it fixated on the last item in any list given in the prompt.
numbers: Prompt listing machines: it often fixated on the last machine listed (3D printer last gave print-everything; laser cutter last gave laser-cut-everything). Authors replaced the list with a general fab lab description. Late in the event it kept iterating one concept when a pivot was needed.
limits: Anecdotal from prompt tests, not counted. GPT-4 era model.
agent_relevance: Order effect in the prompt acts like an anchoring example. Our prompts must not end with a single salient option.

source: Ege et al. (2024/2025) ChatGPT as an inventor: strengths and weaknesses of LLMs against humans in engineering design
finding: Authors' recommendations for LLM in design: use it for ideation, keep human oversight, iterate with feedback, use templates, explicitly prompt for alternatives to avoid fixation, assign subsystem-level tasks.
numbers: Six recommendations; LLM also added unnecessary complexity (KF5) and lost continuity (KF8).
limits: Recommendations are judgement, not tested as an intervention.
agent_relevance: Directly maps to scaffold items: alternatives step, subsystem decomposition.

source: Wadinambiarachchi et al. (2024) The Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking
finding: Between-participants sketching study (N=60): seeing Midjourney images raised fixation on a given example avatar versus no inspiration or image search.
numbers: N=60, 3 conditions (none, Google Image Search, Midjourney), 20 min, 277 sketches (92 in AI group). Fixation score model estimate: intercept -.71; Image Search +.27 (SD .14); GenAI +.32 (SD .13) on log-odds scale.
limits: Visual task, student sample, short 20 min task, example avatar was planted to induce fixation. Authors note results may differ for professional designers.
agent_relevance: AI suggestions can act as anchors. Suggestions that echo the first idea inflate fixation, as in human studies.

source: Wadinambiarachchi et al. (2024) The Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking
finding: AI-supported participants produced fewer ideas, less variety and lower originality than baseline.
numbers: Fluency total effect of GenAI about -.29 (89% CI [-.7,.28]), 76% posterior probability negative; Image Search -.49 (98%). Originality: GenAI -.03 (89% CI [-.06,.00]), 97% probability negative. Variety total effect -.29, 86% probability negative.
limits: Bayesian models with wide intervals; effects small; direct effects after time-on-task were near neutral for GenAI.
agent_relevance: Quantity from AI does not guarantee diversity; measure variety, not count.

source: Wadinambiarachchi et al. (2024) The Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking
finding: Fixation passes through the AI images: sketches resembled the Midjourney images seen just before them.
numbers: Spearman rho = 0.56 between fixation score of AI image set and the next sketch (82 sketches after dropping 10 made before any prompt). Also found fixation displacement: focus shifts from the example to the AI images.
limits: Correlation, not causal; image model, not an LLM text agent.
agent_relevance: Self-anchoring risk: an agent that reads its own earlier output may fixate on it. Break chains with fresh restatement.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI
finding: Proposes that GenAI itself shows design fixation, defined as restricted exploration of the generative space. Tested with GPT-4o (text) and Midjourney (image) chair designs against Red Dot award chairs.
numbers: 10 novice designers (age mean 22.7, SD 3.01), 96 AI solutions; Red Dot set as human benchmark.
limits: N=10, one task (office chair), novice-only, interviews subjective.
agent_relevance: Gives a name and metrics (word novelty, pairwise embedding distance) for LLM fixation we can reuse.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI
finding: Text outputs from ChatGPT were less lexically diverse than human award designs.
numbers: Share of unique terms: 67.4% for ChatGPT vs 78.2% for Red Dot. Structure-keyword rate per 100 cases: Red Dot 208.57 vs ChatGPT 142.71. Seat 66.67 vs 45.83; leg 46.67 vs 10.42.
limits: Keyword counts are a crude proxy for idea diversity; Red Dot data are finished, curated designs.
agent_relevance: Run a quick lexical novelty check on our agent's candidate pool.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI
finding: Image outputs were also more clustered than human award designs on shape, colour and texture.
numbers: Mean pairwise global-feature distance: Red Dot 16.2509 (SD 3.2638) vs Midjourney 16.0503 (SD 4.3814), p=0.0238; shape, colour, texture p<0.01, all larger for Red Dot.
limits: Small global-feature gap; embedding choice affects distance.
agent_relevance: Embedding-distance diversity is a cheap check; the gap was small for global features.

source: Lim et al. (2025) Feed-O-Meter: AI-generated mentee personas for design feedback practice
finding: An LLM persona of a first-year design novice (Alex) with an empty knowledge state, updated only through the session, was used so students could practise critique. Shows LLMs can be bounded to novice-level knowledge.
numbers: 24 design students, within-subject. Expert ratings of 96 sessions by 12 experts: specificity 4.64 vs 4.34 (p=0.0005), justification 4.73 vs 4.42 (p=0.0001), action 4.19 vs 3.93 (p=0.0025); overall helpfulness 4.47 vs 4.38 (p=0.79, n.s.).
limits: Persona fidelity judged by users, 7 of 24 saw it as novice-exclusive; no check that it matches real novice behaviour.
agent_relevance: Empty-knowledge-state trick is a way to simulate a novice for testing our scaffold against novice versus expert modes.

source: Lim et al. (2025) Feed-O-Meter
finding: Authors repeat the claim that novices may passively accept LLM ideas while experienced designers critique them more effectively; their tool let novices critique LLM concepts.
numbers: Claim cited from prior work (their ref 95); no new number for this contrast.
limits: Secondhand claim, not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Expertise acts as the evaluation filter on LLM suggestions; an agent without one needs an explicit critic stage.

source: Shaer et al. (2024) AI-Augmented Brainwriting: Investigating the use of LLMs in group ideation
finding: GPT-4 as idea rater was moderately self-consistent but more generous than humans, and agreed with expert and novice rankings about as much as they agreed with each other.
numbers: 148 ideas rated by 3 experts, 6 novices, GPT-4 (29 repeats). Fleiss kappa: relevance .42, innovation .40, insightfulness .49. Pearson of rankings: expert-GPT-4 .556, novice-GPT-4 .547, expert-novice .602. GPT-4 mean rating 4.19 relevance, 3.72 innovation, 3.68 insightfulness.
limits: Small rater pools; experts were HCI researchers; GPT-4 used 5 much more often than humans.
agent_relevance: An LLM judge can stand in for an expert only coarsely; best for filtering top and bottom ideas, not fine ranking.

source: Shaer et al. (2024) AI-Augmented Brainwriting: Investigating the use of LLMs in group ideation
finding: Experts were harsher than novices; experts and novices disagreed among themselves with medium-to-low internal consistency. Of the experts' top 4 ideas, 1 was 2nd on GPT-4 list and the rest in its top half; 3 of the lowest 4 were in GPT-4's bottom 6.
numbers: Expert top scores 13, 12.5, 12.5, 12.5 (sum of 3 criteria); bottom 5.75 to 5.25.
limits: Tiny top-4 and bottom-4 samples.
agent_relevance: Experts are more critical; a judge prompted as an expert should give lower and more spread ratings. LLM judge is lenient by default.

source: Shaer et al. (2024) AI-Augmented Brainwriting: Investigating the use of LLMs in group ideation
finding: Group brainwriting with GPT-3 added to the divergence stage of novice designers' ideation.
numbers: 16 undergraduate students in a tangible interaction design course; qualitative and quantitative. Paper concludes LLM integration can enhance both process and outcome.
limits: Course setting, small N, no expert comparison group for generation.
agent_relevance: Novice ideation benefits from a divergence helper; expert generation was not tested.

source: Sankar et al. (2026) Progressive Ideation using an Agentic AI Framework (MIDAS)
finding: 13-agent system built to copy the human meta-cognitive ideation loop (define problem, generate, check novelty against patents and literature, reframe) rather than one-shot LLM lists.
numbers: Six M.Des novice designers, six problems, 20 min per session. Raw AI ideas 50-80 per session; final sets 24, 19, 19, 15, 11, 17. Human-seeded ideas 8,6,6,5,4,6 (Muse agent).
limits: Demonstration, not a controlled trial vs baseline; novelty judged by embedding clustering (DBSCAN labelled all final ideas noise, i.e. none clustered). No expert group tested; authors list it as future work.
agent_relevance: A published agent loop that adds explicit problem definition, a global-novelty check and a local-novelty filter. Close to our O-operators; evidence of benefit is weak.

source: Sankar et al. (2026) Progressive Ideation using an Agentic AI Framework (MIDAS)
finding: Authors argue single-spurt LLM ideation produces semantically clustered ideas and a novelty illusion (interpolation of the training median, no check against prior art).
numbers: Claim backed by their earlier embedding work (ref 18); this paper reports no head-to-head numbers.
limits: Position claim; stated as the paper's motivation.
agent_relevance: Supports adding a prior-art and duplicate filter stage after generation.

source: Bruggeman et al. (2025) Probabilistic Methods for Evaluating Human and LLMs During Design Problem-Solving
finding: Compared experienced designers with GPT-4o on eliciting latent user needs from reviews. LLM reasoning was less sound and narrower.
numbers: 10 experienced UX designers (5+ years) in two groups of 5 for protocols; 30 designers in workshops; 43 participants gave rankings. Soundness: humans about .42-.45, workshop .495, GPT-4o .298. Completeness: protocol variance 2.4e-3, GPT-4o 1.9e-3, prompted GPT-4o 6.0e-4.
limits: Read through a summary fetch of the page, not the full paper; the summary itself flagged internal number inconsistencies. Five designers per group.
agent_relevance: LLM output covers a narrower need space than experts; prompting narrowed it further. Check coverage, not only correctness.

source: Bruggeman et al. (2025) Probabilistic Methods for Evaluating Human and LLMs During Design Problem-Solving
finding: Argues outcome checks can approve LLM output without testing its reasoning, and protocol analysis needs think-aloud that LLMs do not give in the same way.
numbers: Method proposal: score soundness and completeness of annotation-based reasoning.
limits: Method paper; five designers per protocol group.
agent_relevance: Argues for logging and auditing the reasoning trace, not just the final design.

source: Empirical Study of Problem-solution Co-evolution in Human-GAI Collaborative Conceptual Design (DRS 2024)
finding: Retrospective protocol analysis of novice designers co-designing with text and image generators. Authors propose a human-GAI co-evolution model where GAI helps problem framing through abductive reasoning.
numbers: 20 novice designers. Abstract reports no other numbers.
limits: Abstract page only; no effect sizes available.
agent_relevance: Novices use GAI to reframe the problem, not just to supply solutions.

source: Panda (2025) A Framework for LLM-powered Design Assistants
finding: Conceptual framework for LLM design assistants, drawing on Simon's view of design as problem solving and design dialogue. No empirical test on expertise.
numbers: No empirical numbers.
limits: Framework paper, no experiment; text searched for expertise, co-evolution and fixation terms and found none relevant.
agent_relevance: Little help; shows that framework papers in this area lack tests.

source: Dorst and Cross (2001) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution
finding: Origin of the co-evolution model that the LLM emulation work (Zhang et al. 2025) builds on: designers alternate problem and solution exploration and creativity arises when a matching pair is found.
numbers: Not opened this session.
limits: Recalled from memory, not verified here.
agent_relevance: Foundation for the P-S index and transitions used in LLM studies.

source: Maher and Tang (2003) Co-evolution as a computational and cognitive model of design
finding: Earlier computational model of problem-solution co-evolution compared with human protocols. Only seen as a search-result title.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Older AI precedent for coding the back-and-forth as a computational loop.

source: Jiang, Gero and Yen (2014) Exploring designers' cognitive style via FBS-coded protocols
finding: Source of the FBS-based problem-driven versus solution-driven split of designers that Zhang et al. 2025 use as human benchmark. Cited in the AHFE paper; not read here.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Known only through the citing paper.
agent_relevance: Provides the human baseline numbers our agent would be compared against.
